meta.title: Oh a Chord — press one key, get a full chord
meta.description: An iPad instrument where one key press plays a full chord. Chord Type and Modifier buttons set its color, Key Mode keeps you in key, and Strum, Harp and Arp turn a held chord into a part — no music theory required.

hero.h1: Press one key. Get a full chord.
hero.positioning: Oh a Chord is a one-octave iPad keyboard where a single key press plays a full chord. Chord Type and Modifier buttons choose its quality, Key Mode keeps every note inside the key you pick, and a held chord turns into a strum, a harp sweep, or an arpeggio without ever retriggering.

promise.heading: Why this exists
promise.body: Most chord and arpeggiator apps ask you to already know some theory before they're any fun — the right scale, the right extensions, an arpeggiator wired up by hand. Oh a Chord skips straight to the sound: press a key, hear a chord, hold a couple of fingers down to color it, and let Key Mode keep you inside a key without ever needing to know why. The whole instrument is built around one idea — a musician with no theory knowledge should make a good-sounding progression within ten seconds of opening it.

features.label: One key, a full chord
features.what: A single octave sets the root. Chord Type buttons choose Dim, Min, Maj, Aug, Sus2 or Sus4, and Modifiers — 6, ♭7, maj7, 9, 11, 13 — stack colour on top for as long as a finger holds them down.
features.why: No chord charts, no fingerings to memorize. Every Chord Type and Modifier combination resolves to a real, playable chord — there's no dead button mid-performance.
features.mediaAlt: The Oh a Chord panel: Chord Type grid (Dim, Min, Maj, Aug, Sus2, Sus4) and the Modifiers grid beneath it
features.mediaCaption: Slot: Chord Type + Modifiers panel, MAJ lit, a modifier held (screenshot, 1280×800)

features.label: Key Mode
features.what: Arm Key Mode and the next key you press becomes the root. Every press after that stays inside that key — reach outside it and Oh a Chord borrows a sus or diminished chord that still belongs, instead of going silent.
features.why: It's music theory you can feel rather than study — a way to build a good-sounding progression without knowing why it works yet.
features.mediaAlt: The KEY button reading “key: e” with diatonic dots lit across the keyboard
features.mediaCaption: Slot: Key Mode engaged on E, diatonic dots visible on the keyboard (screenshot, 1280×800)

features.label: Strum, Harp, Arp
features.what: Three independent toggles turn a held chord into a part: Strum staggers the notes like a pick across strings, Harp sweeps one or two octaves, Arp cycles up or up-and-down at the tempo you set. Latch holds the chord hands-free.
features.why: A held chord doesn't have to just sit there. These are the same moves a hardware arpeggiator gives you, without ever retriggering the notes underneath.
features.mediaAlt: The performance row: Strum, Harp and Arp toggles, Latch, and the tempo readout
features.mediaCaption: Slot: performance row with Arp lit reading “arp up/dn” (screenshot, 1280×800)

features.label: A full synth underneath
features.what: Behind the gear icon is the same 6-voice DSP core that powers Oh a Synth — oscillator, filter, envelopes, chorus — every parameter live and touchable, without ever leaving the keyboard behind.
features.why: The one-key chord is the front door, not the whole house. Anyone who wants to shape the sound itself can go as deep as Oh a Synth goes.
features.mediaAlt: The advanced settings drawer, slid down over the top of the screen: MAIN, LFO, DCO, HPF, VCF sections
features.mediaCaption: Slot: settings drawer open over the keyboard, several faders mid-drag (screenshot, 1280×800)

features.label: Save your own sounds
features.what: Tweak anything in the synth editor and a save icon appears. Tap it, name the sound, and it joins the preset list — right there next to the factory bank, stored on the device.
features.why: A good sound found by accident shouldn't be lost the next time you touch a slider.
features.mediaAlt: The preset name prompt over the settings drawer, with a lit save icon beside the close button
features.mediaCaption: Slot: the save-preset name prompt, drawer visible behind it (screenshot, 1280×800)

rows.label: Keyboard
rows.value: Single octave; one key press plays the whole chord

rows.label: Chord Type
rows.value: Dim, Min, Maj, Aug, Sus2, Sus4

rows.label: Modifiers
rows.value: 6, ♭7, maj7, 9, 11, 13 — momentary, held while a finger is down; combine by holding several

rows.label: Key Mode
rows.value: Locks every press to a chosen key; off-scale keys resolve to a borrowed sus or diminished chord rather than going silent

rows.label: Performance
rows.value: Strum, Harp (1 or 2 octave sweep) and Arp (up, up/down) — each an independent toggle; Latch holds a chord hands-free

rows.label: Voicing
rows.value: Two sliders move a held chord through the register live, with no retriggering

rows.label: Synth engine
rows.value: The same 6-voice DSP core as Oh a Synth — DCO, 24 dB/oct filter, one ADSR, BBD-style chorus — with a full parameter editor behind the settings gear

rows.label: Presets
rows.value: 9 factory sounds plus unlimited saved presets of your own, stored on the device

rows.label: Platform
rows.value: iPad, landscape only, iPadOS 16 or later

rows.label: Privacy
rows.value: No accounts, no analytics, no network requests of any kind. Saved presets never leave the device

items.q: Do I need to know music theory to use this?
items.a: No — that's the whole point. Press a key, hear a chord. Key Mode is there for anyone who wants to explore a key without knowing why a particular note works, not a requirement to get started.
Not yet. MIDI output is planned but not in this release — Oh a Chord is fully playable and self-contained today with no setup needed.

items.q: Can I save my own sounds?
items.a: Yes. Open the settings gear, change anything in the synth editor, and a save icon appears — name it and it's added to the preset list alongside the factory bank.

items.q: Does it need an internet connection?
items.a: No. Nothing about Oh a Chord ever leaves the device — no accounts, no analytics, no sync. Saved presets are a file on your iPad, nowhere else.
iPadOS 16 or later. It's a landscape-only instrument — chord controls under your left hand, keyboard under your right.
